vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: skillup
Version: 0.1.6

SkillUp is a legitimate automation utility designed to check, package, and publish OpenClaw skills to platforms including GitHub, Xiaping, and ClawHub. The bundle consists of shell scripts that utilize standard tools (curl, git, zip, python3) and official CLIs (gh, claw, clawhub) to manage skill metadata and perform uploads. While the scripts handle sensitive API tokens and perform network requests, these actions are transparently documented and strictly aligned with the tool's stated purpose of cross-platform skill distribution. No evidence of data exfiltration, unauthorized persistence, or malicious prompt injection was found.

llm.summary: The skill's requirements, scripts, and runtime instructions are coherent with its stated purpose of packaging and publishing skills to GitHub, 虾评 (Xiaping), OpenClaw, and ClawHub; the requested CLI tools and environment variables match those targets and no unrelated secrets or system paths are accessed.

dimensions.detail: The name/description describe a cross-platform skill publisher. The required binaries (git, gh, curl, claw, clawhub, zip/python3) and the four platform-specific environment variables map directly to the platforms the tool claims to support (GitHub, Xiaping, OpenClaw, ClawHub). Nothing requested (binaries or env vars) appears unrelated to publishing skills.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md and the included shell scripts describe and implement discovery, validation, packaging, and per-platform publish flows. The runtime steps read declared env vars and an optional TOML config, write artifacts to a configurable artifact directory, write logs into /tmp, and POST artifacts to configured platform endpoints. The instructions do not attempt to read wider system files, shell history, or other unrelated credentials, and operations are scoped to the source directory, config, and artifact outputs.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no separate install spec — the skill is instruction-first but includes shell scripts in the package. No external downloads or extract steps are invoked by an installer; runtime uses system CLIs already required to be present. This keeps install risk low; the code is plain shell and small Python snippets, readable in the package.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill asks for one credential per target platform (SKILLUP_GITHUB_TOKEN, SKILLUP_XIAPING_API_KEY, SKILLUP_OPENCLAW_TOKEN, SKILLUP_CLAWHUB_TOKEN) plus a fallback CLAWHUB_TOKEN. These map to the platforms it publishes to and are justified. Primary credential is GitHub token, consistent with creating/updating repos/releases. No unrelated SECRET/PASSWORD variables are requested.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: always:false (not force-included) and model invocation is allowed (default). The skill does not attempt to modify other skills' configs or system-wide agent settings; its effects are limited to packaging, writing artifacts, and performing publishes to configured endpoints. No privileged persistence is requested.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
This package appears to do what it says, but take these precautions before installing:
- Review and restrict token scopes: give the GitHub token only the minimum scopes needed (e.g., repo or repo:status depending on use), and similarly limit the other platform API keys.
- Confirm platform endpoints: the default Xiaping/ClawHub base URLs are in config.example.toml — verify you trust those endpoints before supplying keys.
- Run a dry-run first: use --dry-run and an isolated artifact_dir to verify behavior before allowing network publishes.
- Inspect the included scripts: they are shipped in cleartext (under scripts/), so you can audit exact behavior (they log to /tmp and may push to configured repos or call HTTP upload endpoints).
- Use a least-privilege environment: consider running initial tests inside a disposable account or container so inadvertent pushes are contained.
- If you plan to let an autonomous agent invoke this skill, be aware it can perform remote uploads using supplied tokens — only enable autonomous use if you trust the agent policy and the provided credentials.
